procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 06/07.10.2015 of the High Court of Gujarat at Ahmedabad in Criminal Revision Application No.778
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings:
1. Appellants filed a petition before the Bombay High Court, being Writ Petition (Criminal) No.173/2014, for quashing of the FIR and for setting aside the freezing order which, however, was rejected on 4th November, 2014 with liberty to the appellants to approach the jurisdictional court.
2. Appellants then filed Special Criminal Application No.2710/2014 before the High Court No.338/2015 and is pending for consideration by a larger Bench in terms of order dated 19th March, 2015. The appellants have been given interim protection of stay of arrest during the pendency of the said appeal.
3. Appellants filed four separate revision applications before the High Court of Gujarat at Ahmedabad, bearing Criminal Revision Application Nos.249-252 of 2015.
4. The anticipatory bail application filed by the appellants in connection with the alleged offence came to be rejected by the High Court by a speaking order dated 12th February, 2015.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture:
1. Appellants preferred special leave petition before this Court, being Special Leave Petition (Criminal) No.3330/2014, which was allowed to be withdrawn on 5th May, 2014 with liberty to the appellants to move before the Competent Authority.
2. The order rejecting anticipatory bail has been challenged by way of Special Leave Petition (Criminal) No.1512/2015 which has been converted into Criminal Appeal No. 1099 of 2017.

issue.issue_text: Whether the seizure of bank accounts was illegal in the absence of prior notice.

facts: The petitioners' bank accounts were seized by an Investigating Officer.
The petitioners argued that this seizure was illegal because they were not given any notice before the action was taken.
law: The court examined Section 102 of the Criminal Procedure Code.
The court found that there is nothing in Section 102 that mandates giving prior notice to an account holder before their bank account is seized.

The court cited with approval a Full Bench judgment of the Bombay High Court which held that Section 102 does not require the issuance of a notice to a person before or simultaneously with the action of attaching their bank account.
application: The court applied its interpretation of Section 102 to the petitioners' case.

It reasoned that requiring prior notice would defeat the purpose of the law, as it would allow an accused person to withdraw the money before the account could be frozen, rendering the court powerless.
Since the law does not require prior notice, the investigating officer's failure to provide one did not make the seizure illegal.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument and concluded that the seizure of the bank accounts was not illegal, as Section 102 of the Criminal Procedure Code does not require prior notice to be given to the account holder.

issue.issue_text: Whether the action of freezing bank accounts was illegal due to the absence of the required intimation to the concerned Magistrate.

facts: The court noted that the procedure for freezing the bank accounts had been followed correctly.
Specifically, intimation regarding the seizure of the accounts was sent to the concerned Magistrate as required by Section 102 of the Code.
The court also observed that the petitioners' own lawyer had "fairly not pressed the said argument" because the record showed that the intimation had been sent.
law: Section 102 of the Code requires that when a police officer seizes property (which can include freezing a bank account), intimation must be given to the concerned Magistrate.
application: The court examined the record and found that the investigating authority had complied with the legal requirement by sending the necessary intimation to the Magistrate.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the freezing of the bank accounts was illegal. It found that, contrary to the petitioners' claim, the required intimation of the seizure had in fact been sent to the concerned Magistrate, thereby satisfying the procedural requirements of Section 102 of the Code.

issue.issue_text: Whether the bank accounts could be frozen indefinitely, or if the investigation's objective could be met by requiring the petitioners to execute a bond.

facts.fact: The petitioners argued that their bank accounts could not be frozen indefinitely and that the investigation's objective could be met by having them execute a bond.
The investigating agency countered that the investigation was still in progress, the petitioners were not fully cooperating, and there were prima facie suspicions of misuse of funds.
The court found that the accounts were under a "serious cloud of doubt" based on discrepancies noticed by the investigating agency.

law.law: The court's role at the investigation stage is not to conduct a trial, but to determine if there is sufficient material for the investigating agency to justify freezing accounts under Section 102 of the Cr.P.C.
After an investigation is complete and a police report is submitted, the affected party can apply to the concerned court for de-freezing the accounts under sub-Section (3) of Section 102 of the Code.

application.application: The Court determined that given the serious doubts surrounding the accounts, freezing them was the "only remedy" available to the investigating agency at that stage.
The Court clarified that the freeze was not indefinite. It was linked to the duration of the investigation.
The Court explicitly outlined the proper procedure for the petitioners: they could apply to the court to de-freeze the accounts once the investigation was complete.
The Court also noted that the Investigating Officer had the discretion to de-freeze the accounts at any stage if satisfied with the petitioners' explanations.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioners' argument, concluding that the alternative of executing a bond was not appropriate. The Court held that because the investigation was ongoing and the accounts were under a serious cloud of doubt, freezing them was the only suitable remedy. The Court clarified that the freeze was not indefinite, as the petitioners would have the opportunity to apply for the accounts to be de-frozen once the investigation was complete.

issue.issue_text: Whether the freezing of accounts could only be resorted to as a sequel to a crime and not for the purpose of discovering a crime.

facts: The petitioners argued that their bank accounts were frozen for the purpose of discovering a crime, which they contended was illegal.
They claimed that freezing accounts should only be permissible as a 'sequel to a crime' (i.e., after a crime has been established) and not as a tool for investigation.
law: Under Section 102 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.), a police officer can seize any property which may be found under circumstances that create a 'suspicion of the commission of any offence'.
application: The Court found the distinction between freezing accounts as a 'sequel to crime' versus for the 'discovery of crime' to be insignificant, particularly when an investigation has already progressed and gathered substantial material.
It reasoned that accepting the petitioners' argument at that stage would advance 'public injustice' and could 'paralyze the investigation'.
The Court held that the crucial factor is not whether the crime is fully proven, but whether there are circumstances creating a 'suspicion' that an offense has been committed.
Since the investigating agency had gathered material that created such suspicion, the seizure of the bank accounts was considered a legitimate step in the investigation process.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that it is permissible to freeze bank accounts based on a reasonable suspicion of the commission of an offense as part of an ongoing investigation. The Court decided it was insignificant whether the freezing was a 'sequel to a crime' or for the 'discovery of a crime', as long as there was sufficient material to justify the suspicion.

issue.issue_text: Whether the continued seizure of the bank accounts was unnecessary as they were not connected to the proceeds of the crime.

facts: The appellants argued that to justify freezing their bank accounts, the investigating authority must show that the money is connected to the commission of the offense.
The Investigating Officer, however, was of the view that transactions from the bank accounts created a suspicion of the commission of an offense.
The investigation was still in progress at the time of the decision.
law: The Court held that it is a misconception to argue that a seizure under Section 102 of the Cr.P.C. is valid only if the account in question contains the proceeds of a crime.
The Court clarified that a bank account can be seized if it is found under circumstances that create a "suspicion of the commission of any offence."
application: The Court found that the Investigating Officer was in possession of materials that pointed to circumstances creating a suspicion of the commission of an offense.
Because this legal standard of "suspicion" was met, the Investigating Officer could legitimately exercise their power under Section 102 of the Code to seize the bank accounts.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the seizure was unnecessary. It concluded that the seizure of a bank account is justified as long as there are circumstances creating a suspicion of the commission of an offense; it is not necessary to prove that the account contains the actual proceeds of the crime.

issue.issue_text: Whether the action of the Investigating Officer in freezing the bank accounts was justified and whether the lower courts were correct in rejecting the request for de-freezing them.

facts: The Investigating Officer (IO) froze the bank accounts of the appellants, who were trustees of trusts, in connection with an investigation into the alleged misuse of funds meant for riot victims.
The investigation was still in its early stages and in progress at the time of the appeal.
The lower courts (Magistrate and High Court) had previously rejected the appellants' request to de-freeze the accounts.
The Magistrate found that a preliminary investigation revealed substantial discrepancies, unaudited accounts, and suspicious large withdrawals, justifying the freeze.

The appellants argued that the accounts had no connection to the alleged crime and that the freezing was an attempt to stifle their activities. They also contended they were not cooperating with the investigation.
law: Under Section 102 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.), an Investigating Officer has the power to seize property, including freezing a bank account, if they possess materials that create a suspicion of the commission of an offence.
application: The Supreme Court determined that it was inappropriate for the judiciary to analyze the detailed accounts and vouchers while the investigation was still ongoing. The appellants' explanations should first be provided to the investigating agency.

The Court found that the IO's action was legally justified because they possessed material that pointed to circumstances creating a suspicion of a crime, thus validating the use of power under Section 102 of the Code.

The Court dismissed the appellants' technical argument about whether the freezing was a 'sequel to crime' or for the 'discovery of crime', stating that this distinction was insignificant at this stage of the investigation.

The Court reasoned that de-freezing the accounts prematurely would 'paralyze the investigation' and would be contrary to the interests of justice, given the suspicion surrounding the appropriation of huge funds.

The Court clarified that the appellants were not left without a remedy. They could apply for de-freezing again at a later, more appropriate stage, such as upon the completion of the investigation, as provided for in Section 102(3) of the Code.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appeal and upheld the lower courts' decisions, concluding that the action of the Investigating Officer in freezing the bank accounts was justified. The Court held that since the investigation was still in progress and there was sufficient material to create suspicion of a crime, it was not appropriate to de-freeze the accounts, as doing so would hinder the investigation.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the seizure of bank accounts was illegal in the absence of prior notice.
appellant_arguments: The seizure of the bank accounts was illegal because it was done without providing prior notice to the account holders.
respondent_arguments: The law does not mandate prior notice for freezing bank accounts during an investigation, as it could defeat the purpose by allowing the accused to move the funds.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the action of freezing bank accounts was illegal due to the absence of the required intimation to the concerned Magistrate.
appellant_arguments: The freezing of the accounts was illegal as the investigating officer failed to provide the required intimation to the concerned Magistrate. (However, the text notes that the counsel for the petitioners 'fairly not pressed the said argument'.)
respondent_arguments: The investigating officer complied with the legal requirement by submitting a report about the freezing of the accounts to the concerned Magistrate.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the bank accounts could be frozen indefinitely, or if the investigation's objective could be met by requiring the petitioners to execute a bond.
appellant_arguments: The bank accounts should not be frozen indefinitely, and the objective of the investigation could be satisfied by requiring the petitioners to execute a bond.
respondent_arguments: Executing a bond would be insufficient, and the continued freezing of the accounts is necessary for the purpose of the investigation.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the freezing of accounts could only be resorted to as a sequel to a crime and not for the purpose of discovering a crime.
appellant_arguments: The power to freeze bank accounts can only be used as a consequence of a crime having been established, not as a tool for discovering if a crime has been committed.
respondent_arguments: Freezing accounts is a valid investigative tool to prevent the dissipation of funds that are suspected to be connected to a crime under investigation.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the continued seizure of the bank accounts was unnecessary as they were not connected to the proceeds of the crime.
appellant_arguments: The continued seizure is unnecessary because the funds in the accounts are not connected to the proceeds of any crime, and the transactions can be justified.
respondent_arguments: The seizure is necessary as there is material suggesting a link between the accounts and the crime. For instance, funds were transferred from a Trust to the personal accounts of the petitioners, and it cannot be presumed that these funds were not for private purposes.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the action of the Investigating Officer in freezing the bank accounts was justified and whether the lower courts were correct in rejecting the request for de-freezing them.
appellant_arguments: The Investigating Officer's action of freezing the accounts was unjustified, and the lower courts erred in rejecting the request to de-freeze them. The petitioners offered justifications for the transactions in the accounts.
respondent_arguments: The freezing of the accounts was justified based on the material in the possession of the investigating agency concerning the accounts and the conduct of the petitioners, such as the transfer of funds from a Trust to personal accounts.

cases.case_name: State of Maharashtra v. Tapas D. Neogy
cases.principle: To resolve divergent views on whether the power of seizure under Section 102 of the Code of Criminal Procedure extends to a bank account of the accused.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The provided text does not contain a complete statement of the binding legal rule; it only references that the court expounded the legal position regarding the power of seizure.
obiter: It is clarified that at an appropriate stage or upon completion of the investigation, if the Investigating Officer is satisfied with the explanation offered by the appellants and is of the opinion that continuance of the seizure of the stated bank accounts or any one of them is not necessary, he may issue instruction in that behalf.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Given the collection of substantial and serious material by the investigating agency which places the entire corpus of the accounts under a cloud of doubt, the Investigating Officer was justified in freezing the accounts based on a suspicion of the commission of an offence. At this advanced stage of the investigation, interfering with the seizure would paralyze the investigation and advance public injustice rather than serving the ends of justice.
legal_tests_applied: The power to seize a bank account under Section 102 of the Cr.P.C. is justified if the account is found under circumstances creating a suspicion of the commission of any offence.
why_appellant_lost: The petitioners' argument that their explanations for the financial transactions should be accepted was rejected because such explanations are a matter of defence to be considered at a later stage, not a basis for de-freezing accounts during an active investigation.

The argument that a bond would be a suitable alternative was rejected because securing the public interest, not just money, is the central consideration, and a bond would not serve the purpose of the law when the entire account is under suspicion.

The court found it insignificant to determine whether the freezing was a sequel to a crime or for discovering a crime, stating that to accept such an argument at a material stage of the investigation would advance public injustice.

The petitioners' complaint about the inconvenience caused by the freezing of accounts was dismissed, as the court held that the law must be allowed to take its course, even at the cost of causing inconvenience to the accused.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's action was justified because the Investigating Officer acted on the belief that circumstances emerging from the bank transactions created a suspicion of the commission of an offence.

The respondent successfully argued that freezing was the only remedy because prima facie the entire accounts were in serious clouds of doubt, and the agency needed to ascertain the extent of the tainted accounts.
The respondent's position was validated by the court's finding that substantial material had been collected by the investigating agency, justifying the action under Section 102 of Cr.P.C.

The court accepted the respondent's contention that there was a suspicion of public donations being used for personal purposes, which needed to be investigated, and that the petitioners had not provided sufficient proof to counter this.
policy_considerations: De-freezing accounts based on the appellant's arguments may paralyze the investigation, which cannot be approved as an act 'in the interest of justice.'
Accepting the appellant's arguments at this stage would advance public injustice rather than serving the ends of justice.
Securing the public interest rather than money is the central point of consideration when theft or manipulation of accounts meant for the beneficiaries, is alleged.
The law must be allowed to take its own course, even at the cost of causing inconvenience to the accused or others.
